analysis.title: US confidence bounces on fuel price drop and election clarity
key_insights: Conference Board consumer confidence jumped to 103.3 in November from 91.9, far above the 92.4 consensus and the highest individual forecast of 94.7.
Expectations component rose 13 points and current conditions rose 10 points.
The bounce closes the gap between sentiment and spending seen over the past two years. Confidence is now roughly consistent with spending growth of around 2%.
ING sees no extra impetus that would prompt upward revisions to growth forecasts.
Gasoline prices fell from a September peak of $4.49/gallon to $3.62, and jobs market readings were stronger, both likely supporting sentiment.
Midterm election outcomes lifted sentiment among Democrats and Independents, while Republican sentiment fell modestly.
The University of Michigan measure did not show the same improvement, so caution is warranted.

K-shaped consumer: high-income households are strong on wealth gains and job security, while middle and lower income households face pressure from rising card and auto loan delinquencies and weak wage gains in a low hire, low fire economy.
Top 20% of households by income account for about 40% of spending per BLS, and possibly as much as 60% per Moody's Analytics, leaving spending vulnerable to a stock market correction.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Large upside surprise that closes the sentiment-spending gap but does not by itself raise growth forecasts.
Actual print beat consensus by about 11 points.

macro_indicators.indicator: US national average retail gasoline price
macro_indicators.interpretation: Falling fuel costs give households relief and support sentiment.

risk_factors: Stock market correction would hit high-income household spending, which drives consumption.
Financial squeeze on middle and lower income households, with rising credit card and auto loan delinquencies.
Michigan sentiment remains weak, suggesting the Conference Board bounce may be unreliable.
Income expectations over the next six months softened.
vol_and_positioning: ING notes a turbulent couple of weeks for stock markets, and flags spending vulnerability to a stock market correction given reliance on high-income households.
cross_bank_references: Moody's Analytics suggests top 20% of households could account for as much as 60% of spending, vs BLS data of around 40%.

tension_points.bull_case: Confidence jumped to 103.3 on lower gasoline prices, better jobs readings and election clarity, and falling energy prices should provide further relief.
tension_points.bear_case: Michigan sentiment did not improve, middle and lower income households are squeezed, and spending relies on high-income households exposed to equities.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A stock market correction that hits high-income household spending.

theme_stances.key_argument: High-income households drive spending while middle and lower income households are squeezed, leaving consumption vulnerable to a stock market correction.
theme_stances.evidence: The K-shaped consumer story still resonates in that high-income households are in great shape
